How readily the ancient instructions transform the people! And when their profundity and subtlety are such as these, how could one fail to apply them? The intent of King Cheng’s address to Jun Chen was as follows: In seeking good government, the essential thing is to do what benefits the people, and the first priority is to model oneself on antiquity. Now that you wish to attend carefully to your office and follow the constant norms, what else is required? Simply this: the Duke of Zhou, as teacher and protector of the myriad people, indeed left instructions to be handed down to later generations. The people cherish his virtue and even now long for him, unable to forget him. From this you can see that what the people desire lies in the Duke of Zhou’s instructions. Take what is recorded in his writings and proclaim it far and near: all of it consists of things under which they were well governed and at peace, and they will naturally listen and obey with one accord. Taking as your basis what is set forth in his ordinances and teachings, promulgate it throughout the realm …

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
皆其習而服之者也自懽然而率從蓋我能如
周公以訓乎民斯民亦以懷周公者懷乎我矣
其訓維何我聞曰至治馨香感于神明黍稷非
馨明德惟馨意以黍稷之馨香不過假此以爲
明禋之具而明德之升聞實所以達夫昭格之
誠是訓也可謂精微矣周公以明德而成至治
也非此訓已然之驗乎爾尚念所治者殷之頑
民旣不可無德以爲感通之本而所由者周公
之訓尤不可無德以爲出治之原思其立言之
===
意而端本以弘化者惟成憲之是遵玩其垂訓
之旨而懋德以敷治者惟舊章之是由期于至
治成而神明格始見明德之感不誣而果非黍
稷之馨矣如是而後謂之懋昭也民之乂也又
奚足言哉抑論民可與樂成而不可與慮始故
繼治世者其道同誠不輕于變更也成王于君
陳惓惓惟欲繼周公之政則二公之治宜較若
畫一矣自今觀之則周公克慎厥始君陳克和
厥中則又若未嘗法周公者蓋與世推移雖聖
punctuated:
皆其習而服之者也，自懽然而率從。蓋我能如周公以訓乎民，斯民亦以懷周公者懷乎我矣。其訓維何？我聞曰：「至治馨香，感于神明。黍稷非馨，明德惟馨。」意以黍稷之馨香，不過假此以爲明禋之具，而明德之升聞，實所以達夫昭格之誠。是訓也，可謂精微矣。周公以明德而成至治也，非此訓已然之驗乎？爾尚念所治者殷之頑民，旣不可無德以爲感通之本，而所由者周公之訓，尤不可無德以爲出治之原。思其立言之意，而端本以弘化者，惟成憲之是遵；玩其垂訓之旨，而懋德以敷治者，惟舊章之是由。期于至治成而神明格，始見明德之感不誣，而果非黍稷之馨矣。如是而後謂之懋昭也，民之乂也，又奚足言哉！
抑論民可與樂成，而不可與慮始，故繼治世者其道同，誠不輕于變更也。成王于君陳惓惓，惟欲繼周公之政，則二公之治宜較若畫一矣。自今觀之，則周公克慎厥始，君陳克和厥中，則又若未嘗法周公者。蓋與世推移，雖聖
translation_en:
…all are things they have learned and accepted, so they will naturally follow with joy. If I can instruct the people as the Duke of Zhou did, these people will cherish me just as they cherish him. What is his teaching? I have heard it said: “Perfect government has a fragrance that reaches the spirits. It is not millet that is fragrant; luminous virtue alone is fragrant.” The meaning is that the fragrance of millet merely serves as an instrument of pure sacrifice, whereas luminous virtue, rising to be heard on high, truly conveys the sincerity that brings the spirits into manifest presence. This teaching may indeed be called subtle and profound. Was not the Duke of Zhou’s achievement of perfect government through luminous virtue an already realized verification of this teaching? You should bear in mind that those you govern are the recalcitrant people of Yin: you cannot lack virtue as the foundation for moving them and reaching their hearts. Moreover, since what you follow is the Duke of Zhou’s teaching, you especially cannot lack virtue as the source from which government proceeds. Reflect upon the intention behind his words: in rectifying the foundation so as to extend moral transformation, follow only the established statutes. Ponder the import of the teaching he handed down: in cultivating virtue so as to extend good government, proceed only by the old regulations. Aspire to bring perfect government to completion and cause the spirits to arrive; only then will it become evident that the power of luminous virtue to move them is no empty claim, and that it truly does not lie in the fragrance of millet. Only after this can one speak of striving to make virtue manifest. That the people will be well governed then scarcely needs saying!
Yet the people can share in the enjoyment of an undertaking’s completion, but cannot share in deliberations at its outset. Thus those who succeed to an age of good government follow the same Way and are indeed cautious about making changes. King Cheng’s earnest exhortations to Jun Chen sought only that he continue the Duke of Zhou’s government; the administration of these two lords ought therefore to have been clearly uniform. Viewed from our own day, however, the Duke of Zhou “was able to be cautious at the beginning,” while Jun Chen “was able to bring harmony in the middle.” It thus seems as though Jun Chen had never taken the Duke of Zhou as his model. For in adapting to the changes of the times, even a sage…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
有損益而協心同道先後實一揆也尤見君奭
善法周公之心
詩
君子至止福祿如茨韎鞈有奭以作六師
陳嘉賓
同考試官教諭楊批機軸嚴整詞華富麗是善
形容周家中興氣象
同考試官教諭王批善言周王安不忘危之心
是有憂治危明之忠者
===
同考試官學正張批鋪張盛世之烈詞整而氣
雄結歸重內脩可謂知本矣
考試官學正何批周王講武遠猷發揮殆盡
考試官教諭艾批舂容典雅
詩人美周王之蒞東都承天休而振武備也蓋
治安之休不可以常恃也周王會同獲福而猶
於武備振之其斯爲保泰之道乎此諸侯美天
子之詩也意謂人君統天下而享無虞之治當
先天下而爲有備之圖吾王今日之舉不有見
punctuated:
有損益，而協心同道，先後實一揆也。尤見君奭善法周公之心。

詩

君子至止，福祿如茨；韎鞈有奭，以作六師。

陳嘉賓

同考試官教諭楊批：機軸嚴整，詞華富麗，是善形容周家中興氣象。

同考試官教諭王批：善言周王安不忘危之心，是有憂治危明之忠者。

同考試官學正張批：鋪張盛世之烈，詞整而氣雄，結歸重內脩，可謂知本矣。

考試官學正何批：周王講武遠猷，發揮殆盡。

考試官教諭艾批：舂容典雅。

詩人美周王之蒞東都，承天休而振武備也。蓋治安之休，不可以常恃也。周王會同獲福，而猶於武備振之，其斯爲保泰之道乎？此諸侯美天子之詩也。意謂人君統天下而享無虞之治，當先天下而爲有備之圖。吾王今日之舉，不有見
translation_en:
…there are modifications and additions; yet, united in purpose and following the same Way, predecessor and successor truly adhere to one standard. This further reveals Jun Shi’s [?] disposition to emulate the Duke of Zhou well.

The Book of Odes

“The lord has arrived; blessings and emoluments are heaped like thatch. His red leather knee-covering glows brightly, as he rouses the Six Armies.”

Chen Jiabin

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: “The composition’s framework is rigorous and orderly, and its language rich and splendid. It aptly portrays the atmosphere of the Zhou dynasty’s resurgence.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: “It aptly expresses the Zhou king’s disposition never to forget danger amid security. It shows the loyalty of one who remains concerned amid good order and alert to danger amid enlightened rule [?].”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, School Director: “It expansively celebrates the achievements of a flourishing age. Its language is orderly and its spirit vigorous. Its conclusion places the emphasis on internal cultivation: this may be called understanding the foundation.”

Comment by Examiner He, School Director: “The Zhou king’s far-reaching purposes in conducting military exercises are expounded almost exhaustively.”

Comment by Examiner Ai, Instructor: “Ample and unhurried, classical and elegant.”

The poet praises the Zhou king for coming to the eastern capital, receiving Heaven’s favor, and invigorating military preparations. For the blessings of good order and peace cannot be relied upon forever. The Zhou king received blessings at the assembly of the feudal lords, yet still invigorated military preparations. Was this not the way to preserve prosperity? This is a poem in which the feudal lords praise the Son of Heaven. Its meaning is that a ruler who unites all under Heaven and enjoys a reign free from anxiety should take the lead throughout the realm in planning for preparedness. Does not our king’s undertaking today show an understanding…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
於此乎是故吾王自鎬京而至洛水之上率諸
侯而舉會同之典蓋大彰夫一統之義而實寓
夫萃渙之機者也但見曠典一脩而百辟協朝
宗之志卜天眷於人心而諸福之咸集殆戩穀
而罄宜者矣新令一頒而萬邦懷拱極之誠徵
帝祉於人歸而百祿之攸同殆單厚而多益者
矣福祿不如茨乎夫福固厚矣肯恃此而無遠
慮哉故垂衣而治非不可自居於逸也然安不
忘危服韎鞈以講武而奭然其鮮明者有以示
===
難犯之威端冕而朝非不可坐享其成也然治
不忘亂服韋弁以臨戎而奭然其煇煌者有以
寓無敵之勢嚴紀律於久廢之餘而聖武布昭
足以鼓六軍之銳氣舉其懈弛者而振飭之俾
皆踴躍以効忠以此禦侮不將遠追維揚之遺
烈乎勗止齊於大閱之時而皇靈赫奕足以倡
六師之勇敢卽其玩愒者而激勵之俾皆奮發
以從事以此敵愾不將遠紹永清之丕緒乎吁
制治於未亂則可弭亂於未萌周王得之豈不
punctuated:
於此乎？是故吾王自鎬京而至洛水之上，率諸侯而舉會同之典，蓋大彰夫一統之義，而實寓夫萃渙之機者也。但見曠典一脩，而百辟協朝宗之志，卜天眷於人心，而諸福之咸集，殆戩穀而罄宜者矣；新令一頒，而萬邦懷拱極之誠，徵帝祉於人歸，而百祿之攸同，殆單厚而多益者矣。福祿不如茨乎？
夫福固厚矣，肯恃此而無遠慮哉？故垂衣而治，非不可自居於逸也，然安不忘危，服韎鞈以講武，而奭然其鮮明者，有以示難犯之威；端冕而朝，非不可坐享其成也，然治不忘亂，服韋弁以臨戎，而奭然其煇煌者，有以寓無敵之勢。嚴紀律於久廢之餘，而聖武布昭，足以鼓六軍之銳氣，舉其懈弛者而振飭之，俾皆踴躍以効忠，以此禦侮，不將遠追維揚之遺烈乎？勗止齊於大閱之時，而皇靈赫奕，足以倡六師之勇敢，卽其玩愒者而激勵之，俾皆奮發以從事，以此敵愾，不將遠紹永清之丕緒乎？
吁！制治於未亂，則可弭亂於未萌。周王得之，豈不
translation_en:
…this? Thus our king came from Haojing to the banks of the Luo River and led the feudal lords in performing the rites of assembly. This grandly manifested the principle of unity, while embodying the means of gathering together what was dispersed. Once this long-neglected ceremony was restored, the many lords united in their resolve to pay court. Heaven’s favor could be discerned in the people’s hearts, and the gathering of every blessing surely brought good fortune and all that was fitting. Once the new commands were promulgated, the myriad states cherished sincere allegiance, like stars attending the Pole Star. The Supreme Lord’s blessings were evidenced by the people’s allegiance, and the convergence of every bounty surely brought abundant benefits and ever greater blessings. Were not blessings and emoluments as thick as thatch?
These blessings were indeed abundant, but would he rely on them and give no thought to the future? Governing with robes hanging loose, he might well have dwelt at ease. Yet in peace he did not forget danger: he donned a red leather breastplate to conduct military exercises, its brilliant appearance displaying a majesty that none could readily assail. Holding court in ceremonial robes and cap, he might well have enjoyed the fruits of accomplishment without further effort. Yet amid order he did not forget disorder: he donned a leather cap to take command of the troops, its resplendent appearance embodying an invincible power. He enforced military discipline after its long neglect, and his sagely martial prowess shone forth, sufficient to stir the ardor of the six armies. He roused and disciplined those who had grown lax, so that all eagerly offered their loyal service. In resisting aggression by these means, would he not recover the glorious achievements of old, when martial might was displayed? At the great military review he exhorted the troops to halt in orderly ranks, and his august majesty shone brilliantly, sufficient to inspire the courage of the six armies. He spurred on those who idled and frittered away their time, so that all applied themselves vigorously to their duties. In confronting the enemy by these means, would he not carry forward the great undertaking of old that secured lasting peace?
Ah! Establish order before disorder arises, and disorder can be quelled before it sprouts. The king of Zhou grasped this principle; would he not…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
成安攘之績而保有周之業乎抑嘗謂武以戡
亂而黷武非所以善治周諸侯之告宣王乃惓
惓于講武而車攻吉日相繼侈一時之盛何哉
蓋天下雖安忘戰必危而況中葉之後又非繼
治世者其道可同也噫善圖治者必有宣王內
脩之實而後可以行宣王外攘之事
豐年多黍多稂亦有高廩萬億及秭
劉鹿鳴
同考試官教諭楊批作此題者不冗則略是作
===
意精詞雅說出豐年氣象宛然在目錄之以式
同考試官教諭王批不事藻飾而詞意自足冲
然有菽粟味佳士佳士
同考試官學正張批豐年景象闡揚殆盡是善
言詩者
考試官學正何批典暢可則
考試官教諭艾批□融氣昌
詩人極言有年收入之富以見神功之當報也
蓋力農以豐登為慶也有年之所入而積之極
punctuated:
成安攘之績，而保有周之業乎？抑嘗謂武以戡亂，而黷武非所以善治。周諸侯之告宣王，乃惓惓于講武，而《車攻》《吉日》相繼侈一時之盛，何哉？蓋天下雖安，忘戰必危；而況中葉之後，又非繼治世者，其道可同也。噫！善圖治者，必有宣王內脩之實，而後可以行宣王外攘之事。

豐年多黍多稂，亦有高廩，萬億及秭。
劉鹿鳴

同考試官教諭楊批：作此題者，不冗則略。是作意精詞雅，說出豐年氣象，宛然在目，錄之以式。
同考試官教諭王批：不事藻飾，而詞意自足，冲然有菽粟味。佳士！佳士！
同考試官學正張批：豐年景象，闡揚殆盡，是善言詩者。
考試官學正何批：典暢可則。
考試官教諭艾批：□融氣昌。

詩人極言有年收入之富，以見神功之當報也。蓋力農，以豐登為慶也。有年之所入，而積之極
translation_en:
…achieve peace at home and repel threats from abroad, thereby preserving the Zhou dynasty’s dominion? Yet it has been said that military force serves to quell disorder, while excessive warfare is no means of governing well. Why, then, were the Zhou feudal lords so earnest in urging King Xuan to conduct military exercises, while “Our Chariots Were Strong” (Che gong) and “Auspicious Day” (Ji ri) successively extolled the splendor of that age? Though the realm may be peaceful, forgetting warfare inevitably brings danger. Moreover, a ruler coming after a dynasty’s middle period cannot follow the same course as one inheriting an age of good government. Ah! Those who would govern well must first match King Xuan’s substantive achievements in internal cultivation before undertaking his work of repelling external threats.

“In a plentiful year there is much millet and much darnel [?]; there are also lofty granaries, holding myriads, hundreds of millions, and trillions.”
Liu Luming

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: “Essays on this topic tend to be either prolix or cursory. This essay has precise ideas and elegant language. It depicts the scene of a plentiful year so vividly that it seems present before our eyes. We have recorded it as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: “Without striving for ornament, its language and ideas are fully sufficient. Its unassuming simplicity has the savor of beans and grain. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!”
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, School Director: “It brings out almost every aspect of a plentiful year’s scenery. Here is someone who interprets the Poetry well.”
Comment by Examiner He, School Director: “Classically refined and fluent; worthy of emulation.”
Comment by Examiner Ai, Instructor: “[Illegible] harmonious [?], with flourishing vigor.”

The poet describes to the fullest the abundant yield of a plentiful year, showing that the spirits’ beneficence ought to be requited. For those who labor at farming regard an abundant harvest as cause for celebration. The yield of a plentiful year, once accumulated, is exceedingly…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
其富焉非神錫之休而能若是乎此秋冬報賽
田事之樂歌也意謂稼穡之勤固存乎人力豐
穰之獲尤賴乎神休今吾有此收入之富其敢
忘所自耶彼百穀之中惟黍秔之性本有高下
之異宜故西成之際惟黍秔之多則知百穀之
皆熟今上帝溥率育之仁而雨暘維時大田之
稼則既同也黍之宜高而寒者吾見其多焉則
凡同黍之性者可知矣維天篤降康之惠而陰
陽以和萬寶之成何甚盛也秔之宜下而暑者
===
吾見其多焉則凡同秔之類者可知矣是穡人
成功而穫之濟濟也均足乎有秋之利同時入
穀而積之栗栗也遂侈乎高廩之儲以廩計之
不特有萬爾也而且維億焉公私極富有之盛
將隨所用而無不給者也是萬億之入皆明賜
之我受矣彼千倉之求又何足擬哉不特有億
爾也而且維秭焉積貯昭大有之祥將隨所取
而無不繼者也是廩之有秭皆美利之咸入矣
彼百室之盈又何足言哉是則豐年收入之富
punctuated: 其富焉，非神錫之休而能若是乎？此秋冬報賽田事之樂歌也。意謂稼穡之勤，固存乎人力；豐穰之獲，尤賴乎神休。今吾有此收入之富，其敢忘所自耶？彼百穀之中，惟黍秔之性，本有高下之異宜，故西成之際，惟黍秔之多，則知百穀之皆熟。今上帝溥率育之仁，而雨暘維時，大田之稼則既同也。黍之宜高而寒者，吾見其多焉，則凡同黍之性者可知矣。維天篤降康之惠，而陰陽以和，萬寶之成何甚盛也！秔之宜下而暑者，吾見其多焉，則凡同秔之類者可知矣。是穡人成功而穫之濟濟也，均足乎有秋之利；同時入穀而積之栗栗也，遂侈乎高廩之儲。以廩計之，不特有萬爾也，而且維億焉。公私極富有之盛，將隨所用而無不給者也。是萬億之入，皆明賜之我受矣，彼千倉之求，又何足擬哉？不特有億爾也，而且維秭焉。積貯昭大有之祥，將隨所取而無不繼者也。是廩之有秭，皆美利之咸入矣，彼百室之盈，又何足言哉？是則豐年收入之富
translation_en: …such abundance—could it be so without the blessings bestowed by the spirits? This is a song of joy in farming, sung when offering thanks to the spirits in autumn and winter. Its meaning is that, although the toil of sowing and reaping certainly rests upon human effort, a plentiful harvest depends especially upon the spirits’ blessings. Now that we have such abundant produce coming in, dare we forget its source? Among the hundred grains, millet and rice by nature suit different conditions, the one high ground and the other low. Thus, at the autumn harvest, an abundance of millet and rice tells us that all the grains have ripened. Now the Lord on High extends his benevolence in nurturing all living things, and rain and sunshine arrive in season; the crops in the great fields have all matured together. We see an abundance of millet, which suits high, cold ground, and may therefore infer the state of all crops of the same nature. Heaven generously bestows the blessing of well-being, and yin and yang are in harmony: how abundant is the ripening of all the precious crops! We see an abundance of rice, which suits low, warm ground, and may therefore infer the state of all crops of its kind. Thus the farmers have brought their work to completion, gathering the harvest in their multitudes, and all enjoy the bounty of a fruitful autumn. Together they bring in the grain and pile it high, thereby swelling the stores in the lofty granaries. Reckoning by granaries, there are not merely ten thousand, but yi—vast numbers. Public and private stores alike reach the height of abundance, sufficient for every use to which they may be put. These myriad stores brought in are all illustrious gifts that we have received. How could the wish for a thousand granaries compare with this? Nor are there merely yi, but zi—numbers greater still. The accumulated stores manifest the auspicious sign of a great harvest; whatever is drawn from them, the supply will never fail. These granaries numbering zi represent the full inflow of rich bounty. What need is there even to speak of a hundred households filled with grain? Such, then, is the abundance of produce brought in during a plentiful year…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
如此由是而祀典脩焉百禮洽焉雖天錫之惠
實神相之力也則夫行報賽之禮以答神貺者
奚容已乎抑農事始咏於豳風繼詳於豐年諸
頌不以小人之事為可緩而每亟言之且致謹
於先農方社之祀焉蓋人君能念小民之依則
憂勤圖治之心自勃然矣矧周以農事開國而
無逸一篇又歷代相傳之心法此所以成有道
之長也迨至稼穡卒痒而周道其衰矣有天下
者其可忽諸
===
春秋
晉欒書帥師救鄭成公六年夏曹公孫會
自鄸出奔宋昭公二十年
馬化龍
同考試官教諭雷批春秋欲世臣必如欒書曹會
而後可用者以其功與賢也此篇體認真切筆力老健錄之
考試官學正何批有斷制
考試官教諭艾批明盡
春秋紀世官有錄功臣之後者有錄賢臣之後
punctuated:
如此。由是而祀典脩焉，百禮洽焉。雖天錫之惠，實神相之力也。則夫行報賽之禮以答神貺者，奚容已乎？抑農事始咏於豳風，繼詳於豐年諸頌，不以小人之事為可緩，而每亟言之，且致謹於先農方社之祀焉。蓋人君能念小民之依，則憂勤圖治之心自勃然矣。矧周以農事開國，而《無逸》一篇又歷代相傳之心法，此所以成有道之長也。迨至稼穡卒痒，而周道其衰矣。有天下者，其可忽諸？

春秋
「晉欒書帥師救鄭。」成公六年夏。「曹公孫會自鄸出奔宋。」昭公二十年。
馬化龍
同考試官教諭雷批：「春秋欲世臣必如欒書、曹會而後可用者，以其功與賢也。此篇體認真切，筆力老健，錄之。」
考試官學正何批：「有斷制。」
考試官教諭艾批：「明盡。」

春秋紀世官，有錄功臣之後者，有錄賢臣之後
translation_en:
…was such. Thus the prescribed sacrifices were duly performed and all the rites fully observed. Though this bounty was bestowed by Heaven, it was truly also the work of the spirits’ assistance. How, then, could the rites of thanksgiving and fulfillment of vows, performed to requite the spirits’ gifts, possibly cease? Moreover, agricultural affairs were first sung of in the Airs of Bin and subsequently treated in detail in “Abundant Harvest” and the other hymns. The work of common people was not regarded as something that could be deferred; rather, it was repeatedly and urgently discussed, and particular care was devoted to sacrifices to the First Farmer, the spirits of the four quarters, and the soil. For if a ruler can keep in mind what sustains the common people, his concern and diligence in seeking good government will naturally arise with vigor. Furthermore, Zhou founded its state upon agriculture, and the chapter “Against Idleness” supplied principles of the heart transmitted through successive generations. This is how it achieved its long endurance under the Way. When, however, “the crops were all afflicted,” the Way of Zhou declined. Can those who rule All-under-Heaven afford to neglect this?

Spring and Autumn Annals
“Luan Shu of Jin led an army to relieve Zheng.” Summer, the sixth year of Duke Cheng. “Gongsun Hui of Cao fled from Meng to Song.” The twentieth year of Duke Zhao.
By Ma Hualong.

Associate Examiner Lei, Instructor, comments: “The Spring and Autumn Annals requires hereditary ministers to be like Luan Shu and Hui of Cao before they may be employed, on account of their merit and worthiness. This essay’s understanding is sincere and incisive, and its writing mature and vigorous. Select it.”
Examiner He, School Instructor, comments: “It shows decisive judgment.”
Examiner Ai, Instructor, comments: “Clear and exhaustive.”

In recording hereditary officeholders, the Spring and Autumn Annals sometimes records the descendants of meritorious ministers and sometimes the descendants of worthy ministers…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
者此見二國之用人得是道矣彼華孫之世宋
奚取哉夫庸施於社稷績載於國史者是之謂
功與國同休戚者也國有功臣則所以免於敵
國外患之加而培其精神折衝之勢夫人亦其
思而不忘者也而可以泯其世乎於晉得欒書
焉胄乎欒枝者也枝之在晉錫膺乎大賂而城
濮之覇業以彰行成於子人而衡雍之載書繼
定所以頌其功者也書也紹之克光前烈繞角
之遇桑隧之還八人之衆無敢撓其專制之義
===
誠世濟厥美晉之諸族固莫之與班也若華孫
以逆臣之後而宋任之主兵使世操國柄豈世
功如欒書耶以書例宋而其失益彰矣夫行負
絶俗之孤貞守堅不奪之大節是之謂賢與世
為軌則者也時有賢臣則所以興廉頑立懦之
風而息覬覦非望之萌天下所以觀其德而化
焉者也而可以沒其後乎於曹得公孫會焉裔
乎子臧者也臧之在曹守節而不從乎衆辭千
乗之大國逃宋而不覲乎王振百世之高名天
punctuated:
者，此見二國之用人得是道矣。彼華孫之世宋，奚取哉？夫庸施於社稷，績載於國史者，是之謂功，與國同休戚者也。國有功臣，則所以免於敵國外患之加，而培其精神折衝之勢，夫人亦其思而不忘者也，而可以泯其世乎？於晉得欒書焉，胄乎欒枝者也。枝之在晉，錫膺乎大賂，而城濮之覇業以彰；行成於子人，而衡雍之載書繼定，所以頌其功者也。書也紹之，克光前烈。繞角之遇，桑隧之還，八人之衆，無敢撓其專制之義。誠世濟厥美，晉之諸族固莫之與班也。若華孫以逆臣之後，而宋任之主兵，使世操國柄，豈世功如欒書耶？以書例宋，而其失益彰矣。
夫行負絶俗之孤貞，守堅不奪之大節，是之謂賢，與世為軌則者也。時有賢臣，則所以興廉頑立懦之風，而息覬覦非望之萌，天下所以觀其德而化焉者也，而可以沒其後乎？於曹得公孫會焉，裔乎子臧者也。臧之在曹，守節而不從乎衆，辭千乗之大國；逃宋而不覲乎王，振百世之高名。天
translation_en:
…This shows that these two states followed the proper way in employing men. But what was there to commend in Hua Sun’s hereditary service in Song? Those whose achievements benefit the altars of soil and grain and whose accomplishments are recorded in the state’s histories are called meritorious: they share the state’s fortunes, good and ill. When a state has meritorious ministers, it can escape attacks from enemy states and external dangers and strengthen its spirit and its capacity to repel aggression. Such men are remembered by everyone and never forgotten. How, then, could their hereditary lines be extinguished? In Jin we find Luan Shu, a descendant of Luan Zhi. During Zhi’s service in Jin, he received lavish gifts, and the achievement of hegemony at Chengpu was thereby made manifest; he negotiated peace with Ziren, and the covenant document at Hengyong was subsequently settled. These were grounds for celebrating his merit. Shu succeeded him and was able to bring further glory to his predecessor’s achievements. At the encounter at Raojiao and the withdrawal from Sangsui, none of the eight men dared obstruct his rightful exercise of sole command. Truly, his lineage carried forward its excellence from generation to generation; none of Jin’s other clans could rank alongside it. Yet Song entrusted Hua Sun, a descendant of a rebellious minister, with command of its forces, allowing his family to wield the power of the state hereditarily. Did he possess inherited merit comparable to Luan Shu’s? Judging Song by the example of Shu makes its error all the clearer.
Those whose conduct embodies a solitary integrity transcending ordinary custom, and who firmly uphold great principles that cannot be shaken, are called worthy: they serve as models for the world. When an age has worthy ministers, they inspire a spirit that makes the avaricious honest and the timid resolute, and quell the first stirrings of covetousness and improper ambition. All under Heaven behold their virtue and are transformed by it. How, then, could their descendants be allowed to fall into obscurity? In Cao we find Gongsun Hui, a descendant of Zizang. During Zizang’s time in Cao, he upheld his principles and refused to follow the multitude, declining a great state of a thousand chariots. He fled to Song and did not attend an audience with the king, establishing an exalted reputation for a hundred generations. All under Heaven…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
下所以仰其行者也會也嗣之克繩祖武待放
而行賜玦而去顛沛之際不敢忘臣子之恭誠
篤守先訓春秋諸臣莫之與並也若華孫以賄
立之裔而宋縱之來魯專主國盟豈世德如曹
會耶以會例宋而其罪益著矣此義行則崇德
報功而厚道敦選賢任能而承弼賴亂何由萌
哉奈何喬木之世既微家父之刺有作由是而
爲三家之專由是而爲六卿之分而僭踰之轍
相尋矣君人者可不深懼之哉
===
夏齊侯衛侯胥命于蒲桓公三年秋八月
諸侯盟于首止僖公五年九月戊辰諸侯
盟于葵丘僖公九年公會晉侯宋公衛侯
曹伯齊世子光莒子邾子滕子薛伯杞伯
小邾子伐鄭會于蕭魚襄公十有一年
宋言
同考試官教諭雷批晉昭平丘之失只當於收束
處見之作者類多冗雜獨此篇明爽簡潔宜錄以式
考試官學正何批嚴整
punctuated:
下所以仰其行者也。會也嗣之，克繩祖武，待放而行，賜玦而去，顛沛之際，不敢忘臣子之恭，誠篤守先訓，春秋諸臣莫之與並也。若華孫，以賄立之裔，而宋縱之來魯，專主國盟，豈世德如曹會耶？以會例宋，而其罪益著矣。此義行，則崇德報功而厚道敦，選賢任能而承弼賴，亂何由萌哉？奈何喬木之世既微，家父之刺有作，由是而爲三家之專，由是而爲六卿之分，而僭踰之轍相尋矣。君人者可不深懼之哉！

夏，齊侯、衛侯胥命于蒲。桓公三年。秋八月，諸侯盟于首止。僖公五年。九月戊辰，諸侯盟于葵丘。僖公九年。公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、齊世子光、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子伐鄭，會于蕭魚。襄公十有一年。

宋言。

同考試官教諭雷批：晉昭平丘之失，只當於收束處見之。作者類多冗雜，獨此篇明爽簡潔，宜錄以式。

考試官學正何批：嚴整。
translation_en:
…all under Heaven looked up to his conduct. Hui succeeded him and truly followed in his ancestor’s footsteps. He waited to be banished before departing, and left upon receiving a jade ring signifying severance. Even amid adversity, he dared not forget the reverence owed by a subject to his ruler, and sincerely and steadfastly observed his ancestor’s instructions. None of the ministers of the Spring and Autumn period could match him. As for Hua Sun, a descendant of one who secured an enthronement through bribery, Song nevertheless allowed him to come to Lu and take sole charge of the covenant between the states. Could his family’s inherited virtue compare with that of Hui of Cao? Judging Song by Hui’s example makes its guilt still more apparent. If this principle were put into practice, honoring virtue and rewarding merit would strengthen generous dealing, while selecting the worthy and employing the capable would secure dependable assistance. How could disorder arise? Alas, once the old established lineages declined, Jiafu’s poetic remonstrance appeared. From this came the monopolization of power by the Three Houses, and from this came the partition by the Six Ministers; successive usurpations followed the same track. Can those who rule others fail to be deeply apprehensive?

“In summer, the Marquis of Qi and the Marquis of Wei made a mutual agreement at Pu.” Third year of Duke Huan. “In autumn, in the eighth month, the lords made a covenant at Shouzhi.” Fifth year of Duke Xi. “In the ninth month, on the wuchen day, the lords made a covenant at Kuiqiu.” Ninth year of Duke Xi. “The Duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, Guang, heir apparent of Qi, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Xiaozhu in attacking Zheng. They assembled at Xiaoyu.” Eleventh year of Duke Xiang.

Song Yan.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lei, Instructor: “The failings of Duke Zhao of Jin at Pingqiu should appear only in the conclusion. Most writers are verbose and cluttered; this essay alone is lucid and concise. It should be included as a model.”

Comment by Examiner He, Director of Studies: “Rigorous and well ordered.”

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭艾批〔得士〕
信好迭講而皆有其善春秋悉美之也此見首
止葵丘之盟于蒲蕭魚之信其有裨於世道多
矣春秋悉書以美之也宜哉自夫盟載掌於周
官而大道之公泯私盟叛於列國而衰世之弊
滋盟非春秋所貴也審矣乃若齊衛之命蒲也
齊桓之盟首止葵丘也晉悼之會蕭魚也而春
秋悉美之者何蓋盟以結信雖非盛世之公而
事有可取者聖人亦不得而槩廢之也以予觀
===
於齊衛桓悼之事蓋有善可褒而不容槩廢者
矣何則于蒲之胥命齊衛相推以牧霸也斯時
也周旋於壇坫之間咸得乎中孚之義即其無
詐無虞之心殆信由衷出者矣古者結言而退
齊衛其庶幾乎至於桓公翼戴襄王而首止盟
焉誓同於八國仰戴乎一人崇正抑邪而惠王
之謀寢子鄭之位定矣俾天下曉然知父子君
臣之倫者多此羽翼之助也及再合諸侯而葵
丘盟焉脩一王之禁令宣五命之訓詞大畏小
punctuated:
考試官教諭艾批〔得士〕

信好迭講，而皆有其善，《春秋》悉美之也。此見首止、葵丘之盟，于蒲、蕭魚之信，其有裨於世道多矣。《春秋》悉書以美之也，宜哉！自夫盟載掌於周官，而大道之公泯；私盟叛於列國，而衰世之弊滋。盟非《春秋》所貴也，審矣。乃若齊衛之命蒲也，齊桓之盟首止、葵丘也，晉悼之會蕭魚也，而《春秋》悉美之者何？蓋盟以結信，雖非盛世之公，而事有可取者，聖人亦不得而槩廢之也。以予觀於齊衛桓悼之事，蓋有善可褒而不容槩廢者矣。何則？于蒲之胥命，齊衛相推以牧霸也。斯時也，周旋於壇坫之間，咸得乎中孚之義。即其無詐無虞之心，殆信由衷出者矣。古者結言而退，齊衛其庶幾乎！至於桓公翼戴襄王而首止盟焉，誓同於八國，仰戴乎一人，崇正抑邪，而惠王之謀寢，子鄭之位定矣。俾天下曉然知父子君臣之倫者，多此羽翼之助也。及再合諸侯而葵丘盟焉，脩一王之禁令，宣五命之訓詞，大畏，小
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Ai, an Instructor: 〔A worthy candidate has been found.〕

Trust and amity were cultivated in turn, each with its merits, and the Spring and Autumn Annals commends them all. We see this in the covenants at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu and the pledges of good faith at Pu and Xiaoyu: they contributed greatly to the moral order of the world. How fitting that the Spring and Autumn Annals records them all in commendation!

Once covenant documents came into the charge of the Zhou officials, the impartiality of the Great Way faded; as private covenants were broken among the various states, the evils of a declining age multiplied. It is clear that covenants are not what the Spring and Autumn Annals prizes. Yet why does it commend all these events: the reciprocal pledges of Qi and Wei at Pu, Duke Huan of Qi’s covenants at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu, and Duke Dao of Jin’s meeting at Xiaoyu? Covenants serve to establish trust. Although they lack the impartiality of a flourishing age, where an undertaking has something worthy of approval, even the Sage cannot dismiss it indiscriminately. As I see the deeds of Qi and Wei, and of Dukes Huan and Dao, they contain merits deserving praise and cannot be rejected wholesale.

Why is this so? In exchanging pledges at Pu, Qi and Wei supported one another in exercising leadership as hegemons [?]. At that time, in their ceremonial dealings around the covenant altar and ritual stands, both fulfilled the meaning of inner sincerity. Their disposition, neither deceiving nor suspecting deception, surely expressed trust arising from the heart. In antiquity, men gave their word and departed: did not Qi and Wei come close to this ideal?

As for Duke Huan, he supported King Xiang and concluded the covenant at Shouzhi. Eight states shared one oath and looked up in allegiance to a single sovereign. By honoring the rightful and restraining the wrongful, they brought King Hui’s scheme to an end and secured the position of Prince Zheng. That the world came clearly to understand the proper relationships between father and son, ruler and minister, owed much to this supporting assistance. When Duke Huan again assembled the feudal lords and concluded the covenant at Kuiqiu, he renewed the prohibitions and ordinances of the sole king and proclaimed the admonitions of the five injunctions. The great stood in awe, and the small …

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
懷皆言歸于好而諸侯之心喻矣俾天下昭然
知脩齊治平之道者賴此約束之功也逮夫蕭
魚會而鄭伯請成焉悼於是時鑒亳北而從武
子之嘉猷禮鄭囚而遣叔肸以播告即其背楚
從晋之久可謂誠在令外者矣昔者城濮之績
豈越是乎是知首止葵丘明道義也而威力非
所計矣命蒲蕭魚尚誠信也而詐僞非所先矣
彼晋昭平丘之盟而以威詐涖之果若是班乎
是故春秋特書同盟以著其競力不道爲後鑒
===
耳彼善有可取而世道攸賴者烏可以是例論
哉噫尊周室攘夷狄春秋教也故齊衛桓悼雖
囿於習俗苟可善焉春秋取之莫非尊攘意也
奈何黃徐不救而桓德衰大夫聽命而君權失
其尊攘之業吾不知所終矣故春秋好而知其
惡其欲有國者敦不息之誠乎
禮記
君子於是語於是道古脩身及家平均天
下
punctuated:
懷，皆言歸于好，而諸侯之心喻矣。俾天下昭然知脩齊治平之道者，賴此約束之功也。逮夫蕭魚會，而鄭伯請成焉，悼於是時鑒亳北而從武子之嘉猷，禮鄭囚而遣叔肸以播告，即其背楚從晋之久，可謂誠在令外者矣。昔者城濮之績，豈越是乎？是知首止、葵丘明道義也，而威力非所計矣；命蒲、蕭魚尚誠信也，而詐僞非所先矣。彼晋昭平丘之盟，而以威詐涖之，果若是班乎？是故《春秋》特書同盟，以著其競力不道，爲後鑒耳。彼善有可取而世道攸賴者，烏可以是例論哉？噫！尊周室，攘夷狄，《春秋》教也。故齊、衛、桓、悼，雖囿於習俗，苟可善焉，《春秋》取之，莫非尊攘意也。奈何黃、徐不救而桓德衰，大夫聽命而君權失，其尊攘之業，吾不知所終矣。故《春秋》好而知其惡，其欲有國者敦不息之誠乎？

禮記

君子於是語，於是道古，脩身及家，平均天下。
translation_en:
…cherished him; all returned to amity, and the feudal lords understood in their hearts. That all under Heaven clearly understood the Way of cultivating oneself, ordering the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world depended upon the efficacy of these binding agreements.

When the meeting at Xiaoyu took place and the Earl of Zheng sought peace, Duke Dao took warning from the events north of Bo and followed Wuzi’s excellent counsel. He treated the captives from Zheng courteously and sent Shu Xi to proclaim his intentions. Judging by how long Zheng subsequently turned away from Chu and adhered to Jin, one may say that his sincerity extended beyond his commands. Could the achievement at Chengpu in former times have surpassed this?

Thus we know that Shouzhi and Kuiqiu made manifest the Way and righteousness, without calculating coercive advantage; the pledging at Pu [?] and the meeting at Xiaoyu prized sincerity and trustworthiness, without giving precedence to deception. As for Duke Zhao of Jin’s covenant at Pingqiu, which he presided over with intimidation and deceit, did it truly belong in the same category [?]? The Spring and Autumn Annals therefore specifically recorded a “joint covenant” to expose their contention for power and disregard of the Way, as a warning to later generations. How could cases in which there was goodness worth commending, upon which the moral order of the world depended, be judged by this same precedent?

Alas! To honor the royal house of Zhou and repel the Yi and Di: this is the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Thus, although the rulers of Qi and Wei, Duke Huan, and Duke Dao were constrained by prevailing customs, wherever their conduct merited praise, the Spring and Autumn Annals approved it. All such approval expressed the intention to honor Zhou and repel the outsiders. Yet Huang and Xu went unrescued, and Duke Huan’s virtue declined; grand officers received commands, and the ruler’s authority was lost. I do not know how their undertaking of honoring Zhou and repelling outsiders ultimately ended. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals recognizes the faults even of those it favors. Does it seek to have those who possess states strengthen their unceasing sincerity?

Book of Rites

“The gentleman speaks through this, through this recounts antiquity, cultivates himself and extends this to his family, and brings equitable order to all under Heaven.”

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
王憲
考試官學正何批說理精明措詞純雅是深
知古樂者錄之
考試官教諭艾批意婉詞暢
賢者明君子論樂之正而因推其效之大也蓋
中和不偏此古樂之所以可道也推之而成脩
己治人之效樂之觀不其深乎此君子有取於
古樂之正而子夏述以告文侯也若曰大哉古
樂之用乎繹其理固有不容言之妙徵諸治實
===
有不可誣之功是故當樂之終而君子聽之可
但已哉八音既闋時則餘音未絶也而嘉樂益
深不覺其揄揚之至萬舞既畢時則遺容可想
也而契慕愈切自極其擬議之真然是語也豈
今之所謂鄭衛之音也耶敬而出之以和真上
古之徽音也所以為英為莖者在是矣又豈所
謂齊宋之音也耶和而濟之以敬真盛世之遺
響也所以為章為韶者在是矣君子之道樂若
此豈徒取聲容之可觀而無補於治化之盛哉
punctuated:
王憲

考試官學正何批：說理精明，措詞純雅，是深知古樂者，錄之。
考試官教諭艾批：意婉詞暢。

賢者明君子論樂之正，而因推其效之大也。蓋中和不偏，此古樂之所以可道也；推之而成脩己治人之效，樂之觀不其深乎？此君子有取於古樂之正，而子夏述以告文侯也。若曰：大哉，古樂之用乎！繹其理，固有不容言之妙；徵諸治，實有不可誣之功。是故當樂之終，而君子聽之，可但已哉？八音既闋，時則餘音未絶也，而嘉樂益深，不覺其揄揚之至；萬舞既畢，時則遺容可想也，而契慕愈切，自極其擬議之真。然是語也，豈今之所謂鄭衛之音也耶？敬而出之以和，真上古之徽音也，所以為英為莖者在是矣。又豈所謂齊宋之音也耶？和而濟之以敬，真盛世之遺響也，所以為章為韶者在是矣。君子之道樂若此，豈徒取聲容之可觀，而無補於治化之盛哉？
translation_en:
Wang Xian

Examiner He, School Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is lucid and precise, the wording pure and elegant. This is someone who deeply understands ancient music. Accept this essay.”
Examiner Ai, Instructor, comments: “The ideas are subtly expressed, and the language flows freely.”

The worthy explains the correctness of the gentleman’s discussion of music and thereby extends his argument to the greatness of its effects. Centrality and harmony, without deviation: these are what make ancient music worthy of discussion. Extended into practice, they produce the effects of cultivating oneself and governing others. Is this not a profound way of considering music? This is why the gentleman values the correctness of ancient music, as Zixia related to Marquis Wen. It is as though he said: Great indeed is the efficacy of ancient music! Unravel its principles, and there is a subtlety that words cannot convey; test it against government, and there are achievements that cannot be denied. Thus, when the music ends, can the gentleman who has listened simply leave it at that? The eight classes of instruments have ceased, yet their lingering notes have not died away. His appreciation of the music grows deeper, and, without realizing it, he praises it to the utmost. The wan dance has ended, yet its movements can still be pictured. His sympathetic admiration becomes ever more intense, and his reflection and discussion naturally attain complete fidelity to their meaning.

But is the music of which he speaks what is now called the music of Zheng and Wei? Reverence expressed through harmony: this is truly the splendid music of high antiquity. Herein lies what made the Ying and Jing dances what they were. And could it be what is called the music of Qi and Song? Harmony complemented by reverence: this is truly the surviving resonance of a flourishing age. Herein lies what made the Zhang and Shao dances what they were. When the gentleman discusses music in this way, could he merely prize its sounds and movements as worthy of viewing, without its contributing to the flourishing of government and moral transformation?

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
吾知其在樂也優柔平中之理既徹其淵微則
其在身也恭敬温文之德自底於純粹情和而
不累於慾也志正而不納於邪也身不於是而
脩乎身既脩矣由是舉而措之家也則樂行倫
清敦睦之風成焉恩以相愛者不至于相瀆也
文以相接者不至于相離也是家齊雖本于脩
身而所以致其齊者一古樂之化浹洽於家而
已矣家既齊矣由是舉而措之天下也則廣樂
成教雍煕之治溥焉道德一而百姓平章也風
===
俗同而萬國咸寧也是天下平雖本于家而所
以致其平者一古樂之化洋溢于天下而已矣
吁古樂之功用至于如此吾君聽之恐臥亦獨
何哉大抵治化之極致固原于樂感然而樂之
所由生又吾心爲之本也誠能審一以定其和
然後比物以飾其節則氣和形和而大和流通
天地且爲昭矣豈但平天下哉故曰先王慎所
以感之者
唯天子受命于天士受命于君
punctuated:
吾知其在樂也，優柔平中之理既徹其淵微，則其在身也，恭敬温文之德自底於純粹。情和而不累於慾也，志正而不納於邪也，身不於是而脩乎？身既脩矣，由是舉而措之家也，則樂行倫清，敦睦之風成焉。恩以相愛者不至于相瀆也，文以相接者不至于相離也。是家齊雖本于脩身，而所以致其齊者，一古樂之化浹洽於家而已矣。家既齊矣，由是舉而措之天下也，則廣樂成教，雍煕之治溥焉。道德一而百姓平章也，風俗同而萬國咸寧也。是天下平雖本于家，而所以致其平者，一古樂之化洋溢于天下而已矣。
吁！古樂之功用至于如此，吾君聽之恐臥，亦獨何哉？大抵治化之極致，固原于樂感，然而樂之所由生，又吾心爲之本也。誠能審一以定其和，然後比物以飾其節，則氣和形和，而大和流通，天地且爲昭矣，豈但平天下哉？故曰：「先王慎所以感之者。」
唯天子受命于天，士受命于君。
translation_en:
I know that, in music, once the profound subtleties of the principles of gentleness, ease, balance, and moderation have been thoroughly grasped, the virtues of reverence, respect, warmth, and refinement in one’s person will naturally attain purity. One’s feelings will be harmonious, unburdened by desire; one’s intentions will be upright, admitting no depravity. Will not one’s person thereby be cultivated? Once the person is cultivated, extend this to the family: music will prevail and human relationships become clearly ordered, establishing a spirit of affection and concord. Those who love one another through familial affection will not lapse into disrespect; those who engage with one another through ceremonial forms will not become estranged. Thus, although ordering the family is rooted in cultivating the person, what brings about that order is simply the transforming influence of ancient music thoroughly permeating the family. Once the family is ordered, extend this to all under Heaven: spreading music will accomplish moral instruction, and harmonious, prosperous government will extend everywhere. Moral principles will be unified and the people brought into harmonious order; customs will be shared and the myriad states all enjoy peace. Thus, although peace throughout all under Heaven is rooted in the family, what brings about that peace is simply the transforming influence of ancient music spreading throughout the world.
Ah! Since the efficacy of ancient music is so great, why should our ruler fear falling asleep when listening to it? The highest attainment of government and moral transformation surely originates in music’s power to move people; yet music itself has its source in our own hearts. If one can truly examine unity to establish its harmony, and then arrange the various sounds to embellish its rhythms, vital energies and outward forms will both be harmonious, and supreme harmony will circulate freely. Even Heaven and Earth will thereby be illuminated—how could the result be merely peace throughout the world? Hence it is said: “The former kings were careful about the means by which they moved people.”
Only the Son of Heaven receives his mandate from Heaven; a gentleman receives his mandate from his ruler.

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
史紀勳
考試官學正何批發揮君臣受命之原融徹
詳盡可以式矣
考試官教諭艾批用意周悉遣詞暢達
記者推君臣受命之原見敬之不容巳也夫君
之命出于天臣之命出于君其責至重矣思以
克承其命容可巳於敬乎表記述夫子之言意
謂天統元氣君統元化其尊同也君奉乎天臣
奉乎君其道同也吾甞稽其受命而知之矣彼
===
天子以一人而操統理之權命若由巳制也不
知君者憲天以弘化者也皇猷之顯設莫非奉
帝則以周旋神化之誕敷要皆本天機以順應
典禮之敦庸固自我出也而究其秩敘之原一
承乎上天之明命焉而我無與也賞罰之用舎
固自我出也而要其勸懲之本一順乎維天之
休命焉而我無爲也是雖於穆默運天固未甞
諄諄然以命乎君也然君之分則統于天者分
之所在自儼若鑒命之我受而不可違矣則夫
punctuated:
史紀勳。

考試官學正何批：「發揮君臣受命之原，融徹詳盡，可以式矣。」

考試官教諭艾批：「用意周悉，遣詞暢達。」

記者推君臣受命之原，見敬之不容巳也。夫君之命出于天，臣之命出于君，其責至重矣。思以克承其命，容可巳於敬乎？《表記》述夫子之言，意謂天統元氣，君統元化，其尊同也；君奉乎天，臣奉乎君，其道同也。吾甞稽其受命而知之矣。彼天子以一人而操統理之權，命若由巳制也。不知君者，憲天以弘化者也。皇猷之顯設，莫非奉帝則以周旋；神化之誕敷，要皆本天機以順應。典禮之敦庸，固自我出也，而究其秩敘之原，一承乎上天之明命焉，而我無與也；賞罰之用舎，固自我出也，而要其勸懲之本，一順乎維天之休命焉，而我無爲也。是雖於穆默運，天固未甞諄諄然以命乎君也，然君之分則統于天者，分之所在，自儼若鑒命之我受而不可違矣。則夫
translation_en:
Shi Jixun.

Comment by Examiner He, School Instructor: “He expounds the source from which ruler and minister receive their mandates with penetrating understanding and exhaustive detail. This may serve as a model.”

Comment by Examiner Ai, Instructor: “The conception is comprehensive and meticulous; the wording is fluent and clear.”

The recorder traces the source from which ruler and minister receive their mandates, showing that reverence must never cease. The ruler’s mandate comes from Heaven; the minister’s mandate comes from the ruler. Their responsibilities are exceedingly weighty. If they wish to prove capable of fulfilling their mandates, how could they ever cease to be reverent? The “Record of Exemplary Conduct” (Biaoji) records the Master’s words. Their meaning is that Heaven governs the primal vital force, while the ruler governs the great work of transformation: their exalted standing is alike. The ruler serves Heaven, while the minister serves the ruler: their way is alike. I have examined how they receive their mandates and have thereby come to understand this.

The Son of Heaven, as a single person, wields the authority to govern all; it may seem that he determines commands himself. What this overlooks is that the ruler takes Heaven as his model in extending transforming influence. The manifest establishment of his august plans consists entirely in acting according to the Supreme Lord’s standards; the far-reaching diffusion of his wondrous transforming influence rests entirely upon responding in accordance with Heaven’s workings. The earnest implementation of institutions and rites does indeed proceed from me; yet, if one traces the source of their ordered arrangement, it derives wholly from receiving High Heaven’s luminous mandate, with no contribution from me. The application or withholding of rewards and punishments does indeed proceed from me; yet, if one grasps the foundation of their encouragement and deterrence, it consists wholly in following Heaven’s gracious mandate, with no independent action on my part. Although Heaven works silently in solemn majesty and has never issued painstaking verbal commands to the ruler, the ruler’s allotted duty remains subject to Heaven. By virtue of that duty, it is solemnly as though I had personally received its overseeing command [?], which cannot be disobeyed. Thus, as for…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
欽崇其命以求無負于天者寧容巳哉人臣以
一身而任輔理之責令若由巳行也不知臣者
代君以有終者也化理之敷宣無非將順乎我
后之德意謀猷之措注一皆奉若乎大君之明
威以一民德人見其典禮之敷也而推其敦庸
之命則受之天子焉而下不敢專也以齊民行
人見其賞罰之布也而原其予奪之命則受之
天子焉而下不敢僭也是雖恭默無爲君固未
甞屑屑然以命乎臣也然臣之分則統于君者
===
分之所在自凜乎簡命之我受而不可忽矣則
夫祗承其命以求無負于君者寧容巳哉夫觀
君受命于天則不可無格天之道道有不盡是
褻天也觀臣受命于君則不可無效君之忠忠
有不盡是慢君也有君臣之責尚其交儆于斯
乎大抵天命靡常爲臣不易克艱之道惟在一
敬而巳君能顧諟天命而存以兢業臣能顧諟
君命而懷以勿欺則上下交而德業成矣噫主
敬之功亦未易言也其端在于養心心純則敬
punctuated:
欽崇其命，以求無負于天者，寧容巳哉？人臣以一身而任輔理之責，令若由巳行也。不知臣者，代君以有終者也。化理之敷宣，無非將順乎我后之德意；謀猷之措注，一皆奉若乎大君之明威。以一民德，人見其典禮之敷也，而推其敦庸之命，則受之天子焉，而下不敢專也；以齊民行，人見其賞罰之布也，而原其予奪之命，則受之天子焉，而下不敢僭也。是雖恭默無爲，君固未甞屑屑然以命乎臣也，然臣之分則統于君者，分之所在，自凜乎簡命之我受而不可忽矣。則夫祗承其命，以求無負于君者，寧容巳哉？
夫觀君受命于天，則不可無格天之道；道有不盡，是褻天也。觀臣受命于君，則不可無效君之忠；忠有不盡，是慢君也。有君臣之責，尚其交儆于斯乎！大抵天命靡常，爲臣不易，克艱之道，惟在一敬而巳。君能顧諟天命而存以兢業，臣能顧諟君命而懷以勿欺，則上下交而德業成矣。噫！主敬之功，亦未易言也。其端在于養心，心純則敬
translation_en:
…how could one cease reverently honoring Heaven’s mandate and seeking not to fail Heaven? A minister personally bears responsibility for assisting in government, and commands seem to proceed from him. Yet this overlooks the fact that a minister acts on the ruler’s behalf to bring his work to completion. The extension of transforming governance does nothing other than support and carry forward our sovereign’s virtuous intentions; the implementation of plans and counsels wholly accords with the great ruler’s manifest authority. In unifying the people’s virtue, others see the minister’s promulgation of institutions and rites; but if one traces the command to uphold and apply them, it is received from the Son of Heaven, and those below dare not act on their own authority. In bringing the people’s conduct into conformity, others see the minister’s distribution of rewards and punishments; but if one traces the command to bestow or withdraw them, it is received from the Son of Heaven, and those below dare not usurp authority. Although the ruler remains reverently silent and acts without intervention, never troubling himself to issue petty instructions to his ministers, the minister’s allotted duty is nevertheless subject to the ruler. Wherever that duty lies, he naturally stands in awe of the charge he has received upon being selected for office and cannot neglect it. How, then, could he cease respectfully carrying out that charge and seeking not to fail his ruler?
Now, observing that the ruler receives his mandate from Heaven, we see that he must possess a way of reaching Heaven. Any failure to fulfill that way is a profanation of Heaven. Observing that the minister receives his charge from the ruler, we see that he must possess the loyalty required to serve the ruler. Any failure to fulfill that loyalty shows disrespect for the ruler. May those who bear the responsibilities of ruler and minister admonish one another in this! In general, Heaven’s mandate is not constant, and serving as a minister is not easy. The way to master these difficulties lies solely in reverent attentiveness. If the ruler can keep Heaven’s mandate constantly in view and preserve it with vigilant care, and the minister can keep the ruler’s charge constantly in view and cherish it without deceit, then those above and below will be in accord, and virtue and achievement will be brought to fruition. Alas! The work of making reverent attentiveness one’s guiding principle is not easily discussed. It begins with nurturing the heart; when the heart is pure, reverent attentiveness…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
立敬立而事天事君之道無餘蘊矣
第貳場
論
帝王治天下之大經大法
劉愼
同考試官教諭劉批文勢波瀾詞旨開闔而議
論變幻悉中肯綮錄之以式多士
同考試官教諭王批據題立說而文詞闔闢曲
盡其妙殆潛心而有得者錄之
===
考試官學正何批議論條暢識見老成
考試官教諭文批剴切古雅可式
論曰聖人所以成天下之治者其有道乎要惟
本諸心而已夫聖人之心何心哉天地之心也
天下同然之心也聖人以同然之心推之天下
而天下亦以同然之心應聖人是以經正而民
作孚法立而民用式而帝王之治斯成矣不然
天下至大也天下之民至弗齊也苟弗自其同
然者以一之卽推之弗準動之弗應其何以立
punctuated:
立，敬立而事天事君之道無餘蘊矣。

第貳場

論

帝王治天下之大經大法

劉愼

同考試官教諭劉批：文勢波瀾，詞旨開闔，而議論變幻悉中肯綮，錄之以式多士。

同考試官教諭王批：據題立說，而文詞闔闢，曲盡其妙，殆潛心而有得者，錄之。

考試官學正何批：議論條暢，識見老成。

考試官教諭文批：剴切古雅，可式。

論曰：聖人所以成天下之治者，其有道乎？要惟本諸心而已。夫聖人之心何心哉？天地之心也，天下同然之心也。聖人以同然之心推之天下，而天下亦以同然之心應聖人。是以經正而民作孚，法立而民用式，而帝王之治斯成矣。不然，天下至大也，天下之民至弗齊也，苟弗自其同然者以一之，卽推之弗準，動之弗應，其何以立
translation_en:
…is established. Once reverence is established, the way of serving Heaven and serving one’s ruler is fully comprehended.

Second Session

Discourse

The Great Guiding Principles and Laws by Which Emperors and Kings Govern All under Heaven

Liu Shen 劉愼

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: The composition surges with wave-like force; its language and meaning unfold and draw together. Its arguments vary in their turns, yet all strike the essential points. It is selected as a model for the assembled candidates.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: The argument is grounded in the topic, and the opening and closing movements of its language fully realize every subtlety. This is surely the work of someone who has gained understanding through concentrated study. Selected.

Comment by Examiner He, School Instructor: The argument is orderly and fluent; the understanding is mature.

Comment by Examiner Wen, Instructor: Pertinent and incisive, classically elegant: worthy of emulation.

The discourse reads: Is there a Way by which the sage brings about good government throughout the world? In essence, it is simply to take the heart as the foundation. What sort of heart is the sage’s heart? It is the heart of Heaven and Earth, the heart shared alike by all under Heaven. The sage extends this shared heart to all under Heaven, and all under Heaven respond to the sage with that same shared heart. Thus, when the guiding principles are set right, the people become trustworthy; when the laws are established, the people follow them. In this way, the government of emperors and kings is achieved. Otherwise, the world is exceedingly vast, and its people exceedingly diverse. Unless one unifies them through what they share alike, whatever one extends to them will fail to accord with them, and whatever one does to move them will elicit no response. How, then, could one establish…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
萬世之經而爲法于天下也哉善乎蔡氏敘傳
曰帝王之治本於道帝王之道本於心知此可
以語帝王之大經大法矣書曰維皇上帝降衷
于下民若有恒性傳曰民受天地之中以生夫
天之所降民之所受皆中也卽皆恒性也恒性
同出于天是天下固無不同之心也惟聖人者
先得天下之所同然者耳而天下之民有弗各
得其心焉維皇降衷之心孤矣聖人爲天地立
心者其能以自已哉故精一執中堯舜禹之相
===
授惟一心而所以治唐虞夏后之民者弗容已
也建中建極商湯周武之相傳惟一心而所以
治商周之民者弗容已也是故舉吾之心以加
諸天下之心而大經立焉大法行焉是經也非
藝極之粗迹也本諸聖人之心而表極於天下
者也率履不越天下之大法在是矣經固不離
於法也是法也非品式之彌文也出諸聖人之
心而丕式於天下者也恒久不易天下之大經
在是矣法亦豈外於經乎經也法也莫非帝王
punctuated: 萬世之經，而爲法于天下也哉？善乎蔡氏敘傳曰：「帝王之治本於道，帝王之道本於心。知此，可以語帝王之大經大法矣。」《書》曰：「維皇上帝，降衷于下民，若有恒性。」傳曰：「民受天地之中以生。」夫天之所降，民之所受，皆中也，卽皆恒性也。恒性同出于天，是天下固無不同之心也。惟聖人者，先得天下之所同然者耳。而天下之民有弗各得其心焉，維皇降衷之心孤矣。聖人爲天地立心者，其能以自已哉？故精一執中，堯舜禹之相授惟一心，而所以治唐虞夏后之民者弗容已也；建中建極，商湯周武之相傳惟一心，而所以治商周之民者弗容已也。是故舉吾之心，以加諸天下之心，而大經立焉，大法行焉。是經也，非藝極之粗迹也，本諸聖人之心而表極於天下者也。率履不越，天下之大法在是矣，經固不離於法也。是法也，非品式之彌文也，出諸聖人之心而丕式於天下者也。恒久不易，天下之大經在是矣，法亦豈外於經乎？經也，法也，莫非帝王
translation_en:
… enduring principles for ten thousand generations and serve as a model for all under Heaven? Well put are the words of Master Cai in the preface to his commentary: “The government of emperors and kings is rooted in the Way; the Way of emperors and kings is rooted in the heart. Knowing this, one may speak of the great principles and great laws of emperors and kings.” The Book of Documents says: “August Heaven above bestowed an inner equilibrium upon the people below; in following it, they possess a constant nature.” The commentary says: “The people receive the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth at birth.” What Heaven bestows and what the people receive are both this equilibrium—that is, their constant nature. Since this constant nature comes alike from Heaven, there is fundamentally no human heart that does not share it. The sage is merely the first to apprehend what all hearts alike acknowledge. Yet if any among the people fail to realize this heart within themselves, the intention of august Heaven in bestowing that equilibrium is left without a response. As one who establishes the heart for Heaven and Earth, how could the sage bring himself to stop?

Thus, through refinement and single-mindedness, holding fast to the mean, what Yao, Shun, and Yu handed down to one another was this one heart; and they could not refrain from applying it to govern the people of Tang, Yu, and Xia. Through establishing the mean and establishing the supreme standard, what Tang of Shang and Wu of Zhou transmitted to one another was this one heart; and they could not refrain from applying it to govern the people of Shang and Zhou. Hence, by extending one's own heart to the hearts of all under Heaven, the great principles are established and the great laws put into practice.

These principles are not merely the outward traces of standards and limits [?]. They are rooted in the sage's heart and set forth the supreme standard for all under Heaven. To follow them in one's conduct without transgression: herein lie the great laws of all under Heaven. Principles are therefore inseparable from laws. These laws are not merely the elaborate formalities of prescribed ranks and rules. They issue from the sage's heart and serve as a great model for all under Heaven. To endure perpetually without change: herein lie the great principles of all under Heaven. How, then, could laws stand outside principles? Principles and laws alike are all those of emperors and kings …

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
之道則亦莫非帝王之心也是故其著於大經
大法之間者曰親九族曰敷五典曰脩紀惇倫
帝王以德教天下者何至焉而莫非吾心之秩
敘也曰粒烝民曰則三壤曰康功田功帝王以
政養天下者何至焉而莫非吾心之懷保也以
至咨岳建牧佑賢輔德克宅克俊帝王所以亮
天下之工也一吾心之權衡也五刑五就兼弱
攻昧庶獄庶愼帝王所以防天下之淫也一吾
心之裁制也仰焉欽昊授時在衡齊政歲月日
===
時之無易俯焉封山濬川敷土墺宅金木水火
土穀之惟脩帝王所以財成天地以盡參贊之
能者也一吾心之經緯也聖人之心旣通天地
民物而無外以故聖人之道自範圍天地而不
過曲成民物而不遺建之爲大經而萬世不易
者此也布之爲大法而四海率從者此也由是
時雍風動綏猷迪德之俗成而天下若其教由
是利用厚生允殖乃粒之利興而天下安其養
由是九德咸事俊乂在官而眾賢和于朝由是
punctuated: 之道，則亦莫非帝王之心也。是故，其著於大經大法之間者，曰親九族，曰敷五典，曰脩紀惇倫。帝王以德教天下者何至焉，而莫非吾心之秩敘也。曰粒烝民，曰則三壤，曰康功田功。帝王以政養天下者何至焉，而莫非吾心之懷保也。以至咨岳建牧，佑賢輔德，克宅克俊，帝王所以亮天下之工也，一吾心之權衡也。五刑五就，兼弱攻昧，庶獄庶愼，帝王所以防天下之淫也，一吾心之裁制也。仰焉欽昊授時，在衡齊政，歲月日時之無易；俯焉封山濬川，敷土墺宅，金木水火土穀之惟脩。帝王所以財成天地以盡參贊之能者也，一吾心之經緯也。聖人之心旣通天地民物而無外，以故聖人之道自範圍天地而不過，曲成民物而不遺。建之爲大經而萬世不易者，此也；布之爲大法而四海率從者，此也。由是時雍風動，綏猷迪德之俗成，而天下若其教；由是利用厚生，允殖乃粒之利興，而天下安其養；由是九德咸事，俊乂在官，而眾賢和于朝；由是
translation_en:
…the Way of emperors and kings, and thus all likewise express the heart of emperors and kings. Hence, what finds expression in the great guiding principles and great laws includes bringing the nine degrees of kinship into harmony, disseminating the five teachings, and cultivating proper order and strengthening human relationships. How far-reaching is the moral instruction through which emperors and kings teach all under Heaven [?]; yet all of it is the ordering activity of my own heart. It includes feeding the multitude with grain, classifying the three kinds of soil, and attending to works that secure the people's well-being and to agriculture. How far-reaching is the government through which emperors and kings nourish all under Heaven [?]; yet all of it is the cherishing and protecting activity of my own heart.

Further, consulting the Chiefs of the Four Mountains and establishing regional governors, supporting the worthy and assisting the virtuous, and placing suitable men in office and employing the talented are the means by which emperors and kings assist the work of all under Heaven: all are the weighing and balancing of my own heart. Assigning the five punishments to their five places of execution, annexing weak states and attacking benighted ones, and exercising care in every judicial case are the means by which emperors and kings restrain excess throughout the realm: all are the discriminating restraint of my own heart.

Looking upward, they reverently attend to vast Heaven and announce the seasons, using the astronomical balance to regulate celestial movements [?], so that years, months, days, and seasons do not fall out of order. Looking downward, they mark out the mountains, dredge the rivers, arrange the land, and make habitable places fit for settlement, duly managing metal, wood, water, fire, earth, and grain. These are the means by which emperors and kings bring the workings of Heaven and Earth to completion and fully exercise their capacity to participate in and assist them: all are the ordering activity of my own heart.

Since the sage's heart reaches through Heaven and Earth, the people and all things, leaving nothing outside it, the sage's Way naturally encompasses Heaven and Earth without exceeding their bounds and brings the people and all things to fulfillment in every particular without omission. This is what, established as great guiding principles, remains unchanged for ten thousand generations; this is what, promulgated as great laws, is followed throughout the Four Seas.

Thus, harmony prevails and the people respond as to the wind; customs of abiding in the right Way and practicing virtue take shape, and all under Heaven follow their instruction. Thus, useful resources are put to work and livelihoods enriched; the benefits of abundant cultivation and sustenance from grain arise, and all under Heaven rest secure in their care. Thus, those possessing the nine virtues all serve, men of outstanding talent hold office, and the assembled worthies dwell in harmony at court. Thus…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
蠻夷率俾慆淫罔縱而庶民和於野由是平成
永賴雨暘時若而天地得其位帝王致治之盛
一至于此孰非大經大法之宣昭也哉抑孰非
聖人以心運天下而天下亦以心孚聖人者哉
何者蓋經法出於聖人之心皆同乎民心者也
聖人固本其民之所自有者為之經與法耳非
於民心之外有加也天下之民亦率吾之所固
有者迪其經與法耳亦非於吾心之外有加也
故聖人因民心以出治即治以天下而聖人無
===
心也天下順聖心以達化即化以聖人而天下
亦無心也故曰聖人之心見於經猶化工之妙
著於物蓋因物付物化工所以盡利以人治人
聖治所以盡神知化工之妙則知聖人之心矣
同前
趙舉廉
同考試官教諭陳 批 理趣精深筆力蒼古是讀
秦漢之文而有得者宜錄以式
考試官學正何 批 不事彫琢而蒼然之光自
punctuated:
蠻夷率俾，慆淫罔縱，而庶民和於野；由是平成永賴，雨暘時若，而天地得其位。帝王致治之盛，一至于此，孰非大經大法之宣昭也哉？抑孰非聖人以心運天下，而天下亦以心孚聖人者哉？何者？蓋經法出於聖人之心，皆同乎民心者也。聖人固本其民之所自有者，為之經與法耳，非於民心之外有加也。天下之民亦率吾之所固有者，迪其經與法耳，亦非於吾心之外有加也。故聖人因民心以出治，即治以天下，而聖人無心也；天下順聖心以達化，即化以聖人，而天下亦無心也。故曰：「聖人之心見於經，猶化工之妙著於物。」蓋因物付物，化工所以盡利；以人治人，聖治所以盡神。知化工之妙，則知聖人之心矣。
同前。
趙舉廉。
同考試官教諭陳批：理趣精深，筆力蒼古，是讀秦漢之文而有得者，宜錄以式。
考試官學正何批：不事彫琢，而蒼然之光自
translation_en:
…the Man and Yi peoples all submit, arrogance and excess are not indulged, and the common people live in harmony in the countryside. Thus the enduring benefits of order throughout the land are secured, rain and sunshine come in due season, and Heaven and Earth attain their proper places. When the flourishing government of emperors and kings reaches such heights, what part of it is not a manifestation of the great guiding principles and laws? And what part is not the sage directing all under Heaven through his heart, while all under Heaven likewise respond to the sage with trust in their hearts?
Why is this so? The guiding principles and laws issue from the sage’s heart and accord entirely with the hearts of the people. The sage simply bases the principles and laws he establishes upon what the people already possess within themselves; he adds nothing beyond what is in their hearts. The people throughout the realm likewise follow what is inherently theirs in carrying out these principles and laws; they too add nothing beyond what is in their own hearts. Thus the sage brings forth government in accordance with the people’s hearts: he governs through all under Heaven, without any private intention of his own. All under Heaven follow the sage’s heart and attain transformation: they are transformed through the sage, likewise without any private intention of their own. Hence it is said: “The sage’s heart is manifested in the guiding principles, just as the subtle workings of creation are revealed in things.” By following each thing’s nature and leaving it to itself, creation brings its benefits to their fullest extent; by governing people according to their own humanity, sagely government brings its wondrous efficacy to its fullest extent. To understand the subtle workings of creation is to understand the sage’s heart.
Same as the preceding.
Zhao Julian.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: “The import of its reasoning is refined and profound, and its writing has an archaic strength. This is the work of someone who has read the prose of the Qin and Han and gained something from it. It should be recorded as a model.”
Comment by Examiner He, Instructor: “It resorts to no ornamental carving, yet its antique lustre of itself …”

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
不可掩論之絶佳者
考試官教諭艾批雄健古雅當是名筆
帝王之以道治天下也本其受於天者也天一
中而已矣人受天之中以生而具於心道之體
也帝王統天立極舉天下有待於其法制使法
立而不本於道道不本於心是亦泛然鋪張之
具而徒以私意擾天下是故經與法者帝王治
天下之迹也中也者帝王所受於天而澄涵淵
懿宰制羣動者也舉其受於天與其治天下者
===
交相流焉而後天下相率以安於法而不吾變
斯其爲帝王有本之治歟蓋嘗觀於帝王處生
民之初矣視天下之生倥侗顓蒙如璞未雕也
帝王且與天下安焉耳而何有所謂經與法耶
迨夫風氣開矣天下日多事矣帝王挈宇宙於
其身而奉天之無私以勞天下則必有措爲法
制而使天下萬世遵之以長治者彼芻狗萬民
者欲殫殘治法一切以虛無導之夫虛無豈足
以治天下哉帝王不然矣然使徒有是經與法
punctuated:
不可掩，論之絶佳者。
考試官教諭艾批：雄健古雅，當是名筆。
帝王之以道治天下也，本其受於天者也。天，一中而已矣。人受天之中以生，而具於心，道之體也。帝王統天立極，舉天下有待於其法制。使法立而不本於道，道不本於心，是亦泛然鋪張之具，而徒以私意擾天下。是故經與法者，帝王治天下之迹也；中也者，帝王所受於天而澄涵淵懿、宰制羣動者也。舉其受於天與其治天下者，交相流焉，而後天下相率以安於法而不吾變。斯其爲帝王有本之治歟？蓋嘗觀於帝王處生民之初矣。視天下之生，倥侗顓蒙，如璞未雕也。帝王且與天下安焉耳，而何有所謂經與法耶？迨夫風氣開矣，天下日多事矣，帝王挈宇宙於其身，而奉天之無私以勞天下，則必有措爲法制，而使天下萬世遵之以長治者。彼芻狗萬民者，欲殫殘治法，一切以虛無導之。夫虛無豈足以治天下哉？帝王不然矣。然使徒有是經與法
translation_en:
…cannot be concealed. This is a supremely fine discourse.
Examiner Ai, Instructor, comments: Vigorous and robust, with antique elegance: surely the work of an accomplished writer.
When emperors and kings govern All-under-Heaven through the Way, they take as their foundation what they have received from Heaven. Heaven is nothing other than the single Mean. Human beings receive Heaven’s Mean at birth, and its presence within the heart is the substance of the Way. Emperors and kings carry forward Heaven’s order and establish the supreme standard; all under Heaven depend upon their laws and institutions. If laws are established without being rooted in the Way, and the Way is not rooted in the heart, these are merely instruments of indiscriminate elaboration, serving only to disturb All-under-Heaven with private intentions. Thus, governing principles and laws are the outward traces of how emperors and kings govern All-under-Heaven. The Mean is what they receive from Heaven: clear and capacious, profound and beautiful, it governs all activity. Only when what they receive from Heaven and their governance of All-under-Heaven flow into one another will all under Heaven follow one another in abiding contentedly by the laws, without turning against their ruler. Is this not the firmly grounded governance of emperors and kings?
Let us consider emperors and kings at the beginning of human society. They saw the people of All-under-Heaven as untutored and ignorant, like uncarved jade. Emperors and kings simply dwelt at ease together with all under Heaven; what could there have been to call governing principles and laws? Once customs and dispositions developed, and affairs throughout All-under-Heaven grew daily more numerous, emperors and kings took the burden of the cosmos upon themselves and, honoring Heaven’s impartiality, labored for All-under-Heaven. They necessarily instituted laws and institutions that all under Heaven would follow for ten thousand generations, securing lasting order. Those who treat the myriad people as straw dogs wish to destroy all methods of government and guide everything through emptiness and nonbeing. But how could emptiness and nonbeing suffice to govern All-under-Heaven? Emperors and kings do not act thus. Yet if they possess only these governing principles and laws…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
而無所以爲之本其受於天與其治天下者憂
憂不相入而惟操其具以率天下也天下其誰
從之不觀之天乎行以四時臨以二曜布以五
行七政若造物者盡是矣而不知一中之主張
流貫於亭毒者固乾坤之所以不毀也帝王以
天道治天下者乃徒操其具而精不流焉豈所
謂以道治天下者哉是故天地未平也而曆象
璣衡封山濬川之法立四時日月未理也而協
時正日之法立人倫未明也而敷典脩紀敘疇
===
之法立典則法制未備也而定賦制刑設官分
土同律度㫪衡之法立帝王之以道治天下而
措設創造者若是乎其井井綸綸枚枚秩秩至
周矣而不知此固治天下之迹也至其受於天
而爲心法之精者又旁皇周浹於經與法之中
而通之天下萬世者也是故精一執中建中建
極堯舜禹湯文武之心法也中以立心心以會
道爲能以天地爲本以太極爲柄以鬼神爲徒
以萬物爲容而澄涵淵懿宰制羣動者冲然邃
punctuated: 而無所以爲之本，其受於天與其治天下者，憂憂不相入，而惟操其具以率天下也，天下其誰從之？不觀之天乎？行以四時，臨以二曜，布以五行七政，若造物者盡是矣。而不知一中之主張，流貫於亭毒者，固乾坤之所以不毀也。帝王以天道治天下者，乃徒操其具而精不流焉，豈所謂以道治天下者哉？是故天地未平也，而曆象璣衡、封山濬川之法立；四時日月未理也，而協時正日之法立；人倫未明也，而敷典脩紀敘疇之法立；典則法制未備也，而定賦制刑、設官分土、同律度㫪衡之法立。帝王之以道治天下，而措設創造者，若是乎其井井綸綸、枚枚秩秩，至周矣！而不知此固治天下之迹也。至其受於天而爲心法之精者，又旁皇周浹於經與法之中，而通之天下萬世者也。是故精一執中、建中建極，堯舜禹湯文武之心法也。中以立心，心以會道，爲能以天地爲本，以太極爲柄，以鬼神爲徒，以萬物爲容，而澄涵淵懿、宰制羣動者，冲然邃
translation_en:
…yet lack that which provides their foundation, then what they receive from Heaven and their governance of All-under-Heaven remain mutually incompatible [?]. If they merely wield the instruments of government to lead All-under-Heaven, who in the world will follow them? Have we not observed Heaven? It moves through the four seasons, shines down through the two luminaries, and distributes its workings through the Five Phases and the seven celestial regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets—as though these exhausted the work of creation. Yet people do not understand that the directing power of the single Mean, flowing throughout the processes of nurturing life, is precisely what keeps Heaven and Earth from falling into ruin. If emperors and kings who govern All-under-Heaven through Heaven’s Way merely wield its instruments without its essential spirit flowing through them, can this be called governing All-under-Heaven through the Way?

Thus, when Heaven and Earth were not yet brought into order, methods were established for calendrical observation and astronomical instruments, for marking out the mountains and dredging the rivers. When the four seasons, sun, and moon were not yet regulated, methods were established for harmonizing the seasons and correcting the calendar. When human relationships were not yet clarified, methods were established for promulgating the enduring norms, cultivating the guiding principles, and ordering the categories of governance. When canons, standards, laws, and institutions were not yet complete, methods were established for fixing taxes and instituting punishments, establishing offices and dividing territory, and standardizing pitch pipes, measures, and weights [?]. So orderly, systematic, and comprehensive were the arrangements and institutions created by emperors and kings in governing All-under-Heaven through the Way! Yet people do not understand that these are merely the outward traces of governing All-under-Heaven. As for what they received from Heaven as the essence of the teaching of the mind, it pervades and thoroughly permeates these guiding principles and laws, extending them throughout All-under-Heaven for ten thousand generations.

Thus, being discerning and single-minded, holding fast to the Mean, establishing the Mean, and establishing the Supreme Standard were the teachings of the mind transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. Through the Mean one establishes the mind; through the mind one comprehends the Way. Only then can one take Heaven and Earth as the foundation, the Great Ultimate as the governing handle, ghosts and spirits as companions, and the myriad things as one’s encompassing form. That which, clear and capacious, profound and excellent, governs all movement is empty, still, and deep…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
矣由是出之以正天度平地軸天下日覆載於
大經大法中而不知帝王以其中爲清寧之紀
也以理四時日月天下日順其寒暑晝夜於大
經大法中而不知帝王以其中爲陰陽之官也
以明人倫天下日惇叙於大經大法中而不知
帝王以其中爲綱常之統也以備法制典則而
使百王有率循焉天下日用於大經大法中而
不知帝王以其中爲古今之會也是故帝王之
道穆乎造物與游而神運四遐若是也夫是以
===
經與法即其受於天者而朗然與風雨晦冥竝
行宇宙也歟孰謂帝王徒以私意擾天下也哉
嗚呼此王道也亦天道也爲而不用運而不宰
有創造而無創造者也繇之則天下治不則亂
者也如權準之行天下而豪商大賈莫得鼓舌
與三尺童子爭低昂輕重也豈惟天下後世不
能低昂輕重之雖帝王亦不能自以已意低昂
輕重之也何者以受於天也故當其時雨暘時
矣山川奠矣鬼神寧矣鳳儀獸舞矣魚鼈若庶
punctuated:
矣。由是出之，以正天度、平地軸，天下日覆載於大經大法中，而不知帝王以其中爲清寧之紀也；以理四時日月，天下日順其寒暑晝夜於大經大法中，而不知帝王以其中爲陰陽之官也；以明人倫，天下日惇叙於大經大法中，而不知帝王以其中爲綱常之統也；以備法制典則，而使百王有率循焉，天下日用於大經大法中，而不知帝王以其中爲古今之會也。是故帝王之道，穆乎造物與游，而神運四遐若是也。夫是以經與法，即其受於天者，而朗然與風雨晦冥竝行宇宙也歟？孰謂帝王徒以私意擾天下也哉！
嗚呼！此王道也，亦天道也。爲而不用，運而不宰，有創造而無創造者也。繇之則天下治，不則亂者也。如權準之行天下，而豪商大賈莫得鼓舌，與三尺童子爭低昂輕重也。豈惟天下後世不能低昂輕重之，雖帝王亦不能自以已意低昂輕重之也。何者？以受於天也。故當其時，雨暘時矣，山川奠矣，鬼神寧矣，鳳儀獸舞矣，魚鼈若庶
translation_en:
…indeed. From this they bring it forth to set Heaven’s measures right and make Earth’s axis level. All under Heaven are daily sheltered and sustained within the great guiding principles and laws, without knowing that the emperors and kings make their inner mean the ordering principle of Heaven’s clarity and Earth’s tranquility. They regulate the four seasons, the sun, and the moon. All under Heaven daily follow the cycles of cold and heat, day and night, within these great principles and laws, without knowing that the emperors and kings make their inner mean the regulator of yin and yang. They clarify human relationships. All under Heaven daily deepen and order these relationships within the great principles and laws, without knowing that the emperors and kings make their inner mean the unifying principle of the cardinal relationships and constant virtues. They perfect laws, institutions, canons, and standards, giving successive kings something to follow. All under Heaven daily conduct their lives within these great principles and laws, without knowing that the emperors and kings make their inner mean the meeting point of past and present. Thus the Way of emperors and kings moves in profound harmony with the workings of creation, its spiritual efficacy reaching the four distant quarters in this manner. Is this not why their principles and laws, being precisely what they receive from Heaven, shine forth and operate throughout the cosmos alongside wind and rain, darkness and obscurity? Who could say that emperors and kings merely disturb the world with their private intentions?
Alas! This is the kingly Way, and also the Way of Heaven. It acts without exertion and moves without asserting mastery; there is creation, yet no creator. Follow it, and all under Heaven is well governed; fail to do so, and disorder follows. It is like weights and standards in use throughout the realm: even powerful merchants and great traders cannot wag their tongues and dispute relative height or weight with a three-foot child. Nor is it merely that people throughout the world and in later generations cannot alter these measures: even emperors and kings cannot raise or lower them, lighten or increase them, according to their own intentions. Why? Because they are received from Heaven. Thus, in their time, rain and sunshine come in season; mountains and rivers are settled; spirits are at peace; phoenixes appear in stately bearing and beasts dance; fish and turtles thrive, and the many…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
草繁矣至是而帝王且以其受於天者贊乎天
矣向使徒法而不本於心則五伯之建樹非不
赫赫也而何以精明果銳之氣一振而無餘味
乎吾故曰帝王之以道治天下也本其受於天
者也雖然帝王之中中於學也彼兢業祗台懋
昭敬止敬義者如天運於上而不少息此聖以
益聖而治益隆也後之君天下者惟務學以致
中則二帝可三三王可四而經與法皆吾心物
矣噫此固帝王純天之治也
===
表
擬
聖駕大閱禮成羣臣
賀表〔隆慶三年〕
徐渭
同考試官敎諭楊批我
皇上保泰之意鋪張殆盡子其亦有先憂後樂之志者乎
同考試官敎諭王批詞藻煥發矩度森嚴是工
於四六者
punctuated:
草繁矣。至是，而帝王且以其受於天者贊乎天矣。向使徒法而不本於心，則五伯之建樹非不赫赫也，而何以精明果銳之氣一振而無餘味乎？吾故曰：帝王之以道治天下也，本其受於天者也。雖然，帝王之中，中於學也。彼兢業、祗台、懋昭、敬止、敬義者，如天運於上而不少息，此聖以益聖而治益隆也。後之君天下者，惟務學以致中，則二帝可三，三王可四，而經與法皆吾心物矣。噫！此固帝王純天之治也。

表
擬聖駕大閱禮成羣臣賀表〔隆慶三年〕
徐渭

同考試官敎諭楊批：我皇上保泰之意，鋪張殆盡。子其亦有先憂後樂之志者乎？

同考試官敎諭王批：詞藻煥發，矩度森嚴，是工於四六者。
translation_en:
… grasses flourish. At this point, emperors and kings can even assist Heaven through what they have received from Heaven. Had they merely followed established methods without grounding them in the heart, then consider the Five Hegemons: their achievements were certainly illustrious, yet why did their keen, resolute energy expend itself in a single surge, leaving no lasting savor? Thus I say: when emperors and kings govern the world through the Way, they take as their foundation what they have received from Heaven. Nevertheless, the equilibrium of emperors and kings is attained through learning. Their vigilance and diligence, reverence for the exalted station [?], earnest illumination of virtue, abiding reverence, and reverence and righteousness resemble Heaven revolving above without the slightest pause. Through these, sages become still more sagely and government ever more flourishing. If later rulers of the world devote themselves to learning in order to attain equilibrium, they can become a third alongside the Two Emperors or a fourth alongside the Three Kings; the enduring principles and governing methods will all be things within their own hearts. Ah! This indeed is the government of emperors and kings in perfect accord with Heaven.

Memorial
Draft congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials upon the completion of the ceremonial Grand Military Review conducted by His Majesty. 〔Third year of Longqing [1569]〕
Xu Wei

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: You have expounded almost exhaustively our emperor’s intention to preserve peace and prosperity. Might you, too, aspire to be first in taking on worries and last in enjoying happiness?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor: The diction is brilliant, and the formal rules are rigorously observed. This is the work of one skilled in four-and-six parallel prose.

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭張批駢麗中寫揄揚之意且典
則可嘉錄之
考試官學正何批美不忘規足占忠悃
考試官教諭艾批雅麗可觀
隆慶三年某月某日具官臣某等恭遇
聖駕大閱禮成謹奉
表稱
賀者伏以
天仗霜嚴
===
聖武應金秋而肅令
龍旂風動
皇靈闡寶曆以宣威仰
萬乘之雲從振六師而虎奮江山壯色寰宇
騰懽臣等稽首頓首上言竊惟國家保治
之機在安内而攘外帝王持盈之要必緯
武以經文唐虞不廢詰戎夏商尤勤簡乘
伐崇遏密文德彌光吉日車攻英聲茂著
圃原習戰日聞車馬之音具囿觀兵時見
punctuated:
同考試官教諭張批：駢麗中寫揄揚之意，且典則可嘉，錄之。
考試官學正何批：美不忘規，足占忠悃。
考試官教諭艾批：雅麗可觀。
隆慶三年某月某日，具官臣某等，恭遇聖駕大閱禮成，謹奉表稱賀者。伏以：天仗霜嚴，聖武應金秋而肅令；龍旂風動，皇靈闡寶曆以宣威。仰萬乘之雲從，振六師而虎奮。江山壯色，寰宇騰懽。臣等稽首頓首上言：竊惟國家保治之機，在安内而攘外；帝王持盈之要，必緯武以經文。唐虞不廢詰戎，夏商尤勤簡乘。伐崇遏密，文德彌光；吉日車攻，英聲茂著。圃原習戰，日聞車馬之音；具囿觀兵，時見
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “The elegant parallel prose conveys praise, while its classical correctness is also commendable. Select it.”
Examiner He, Instructor, comments: “In praising, he does not forget admonition: this sufficiently reveals his loyal sincerity.”
Examiner Ai, Instructor, comments: “Refined and elegant, and well worth reading.”
On a certain day of a certain month in the third year of Longqing [1569], your servants So-and-so and others, holding their respective offices, respectfully submit this memorial of congratulation on the completion of the ceremonies of the grand military review conducted by Your Majesty in person. We humbly reflect:
The imperial armed escort is stern as frost; Your Majesty’s martial power accords with the autumn season of Metal, making commands rigorous. Dragon banners stir in the wind; imperial majesty unfolds the precious dynastic calendar and proclaims its might. We look up to the cloudlike retinue of the sovereign of ten thousand chariots, who rouses the Six Armies to spring forth like tigers. Rivers and mountains take on a magnificent aspect; joy surges throughout the realm. Your servants bow their heads to the ground and repeatedly kowtow, submitting these words:
We humbly consider that the means by which a state preserves good order lie in securing peace within and repelling threats from without. The essential means by which emperors and kings sustain prosperity require military affairs as the weft and civil governance as the warp. The rulers of Tang and Yu did not neglect military preparedness; those of Xia and Shang were especially diligent in inspecting their war chariots. In the attack on Chong and in solemn silence, civil virtue shone ever more brightly; in “Auspicious Day” and “Chariot Attack,” heroic renown was splendidly displayed. When warfare was practised on the garden grounds [?], the sounds of chariots and horses were heard daily; when troops were reviewed in Ju Park, there were seen from time to time…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
羽旄之美降延季世寖墬前脩未閑攻圍
擊刺之方莫辨鼓鐸鐲鐃之用會都試武
技原非有備之謨平樂整軍容奚取不虞
之戒睠茲
令典有待
明君恭惟
皇帝陛下
智勇天授
睿哲性成
===
際百年開泰之期
應九葉重華之運
經筵日御聿昭
文治之光疆圉秋防載纘
武功之緒
嗣丕基於有永
圖至治於無疆爰念
先朝首剙營制與衛閑於部伍樞筦典自勳臣
顧世際承平致人趨玩愒非申蒐閱之令
punctuated:
羽旄之美。降延季世，寖墬前脩，未閑攻圍擊刺之方，莫辨鼓鐸鐲鐃之用。會都試武技，原非有備之謨；平樂整軍容，奚取不虞之戒？睠茲令典，有待明君。
恭惟皇帝陛下，智勇天授，睿哲性成。際百年開泰之期，應九葉重華之運。經筵日御，聿昭文治之光；疆圉秋防，載纘武功之緒。嗣丕基於有永，圖至治於無疆。爰念先朝首剙營制，與衛閑於部伍，樞筦典自勳臣。顧世際承平，致人趨玩愒，非申蒐閱之令，
translation_en:
…the splendor of feathered standards and yak-tail banners. As time descended into the latter ages, the accomplishments of earlier generations gradually fell into neglect. Men were unpracticed in the methods of assault, siege, striking, and thrusting, and could not distinguish the uses of drums, bells, marching gongs, and halting cymbals. Testing martial skills at gatherings in the capital was hardly a plan for preparedness; drawing up impressive military formations at Pingle—how could this provide precautions against the unexpected? The revival of these excellent institutions awaited an enlightened ruler.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses Heaven-bestowed wisdom and courage, and sagacity innate in your nature. You have come at a time when a century of rule opens into flourishing peace, answering the auspicious destiny of the ninth imperial generation renewing its predecessors’ splendor. You attend the Classics Colloquium daily, thereby displaying the brilliance of civil governance; through autumn defenses along the frontiers, you carry forward the legacy of military achievement. You perpetuate the great dynastic foundation forever and seek consummate government without limit. Mindful that earlier reigns first established the system of military camps, with the guards trained in their units [?], and entrusted central military direction to meritorious nobles, you reflect that prolonged peace has led men toward negligence and idleness. Unless the orders for military musters and inspections are renewed, …

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
罔裨乂大之猷特軫
宸衷重煩
聖慮
允輔臣之獻疏斷在必行
諭司馬以陳兵筭無遺策
翠華遙蒞欣瞻
玉輅以臨戎黃道弘開喜見
天顏之閱武羽林星列近羅虎賁三千車騎雲
屯厚集貔貅百萬鵝鸛魚麗迭見縱橫繁
===
弱僕姑各輸巧力雲飛
黃幄鷲𩿨斧鉞流光日映
朱鑾快覩旌旆耀彩師徒驃健同懷裹革之
心將佐鷹揚共奮請纓之義氣橫千里何
須鳴劔伊吾紀肅三營不數屯軍細柳沴
此
揚威伐叛電掃風馳由是
保大定功外威內治允矣承
皇考纘圖之志廓
punctuated: 罔裨乂大之猷，特軫宸衷，重煩聖慮。允輔臣之獻疏，斷在必行；諭司馬以陳兵，筭無遺策。翠華遙蒞，欣瞻玉輅以臨戎；黃道弘開，喜見天顏之閱武。羽林星列，近羅虎賁三千；車騎雲屯，厚集貔貅百萬。鵝鸛魚麗，迭見縱橫；繁弱僕姑，各輸巧力。雲飛黃幄，鷲𩿨斧鉞流光；日映朱鑾，快覩旌旆耀彩。師徒驃健，同懷裹革之心；將佐鷹揚，共奮請纓之義。氣橫千里，何須鳴劔伊吾；紀肅三營，不數屯軍細柳。沴此揚威伐叛，電掃風馳；由是保大定功，外威內治。允矣承皇考纘圖之志，廓
translation_en:
…there would be no benefit to the grand design of governance [?]. This especially troubled the imperial heart and again engaged Your Majesty’s sagely concern. You approved the assisting ministers’ submitted memorial, firmly resolving that it must be implemented; you instructed the Minister of War to array the troops, leaving no stratagem unconsidered.

The kingfisher-feathered imperial standard approached from afar, and we joyfully beheld the jade imperial carriage arriving before the troops. The imperial way opened wide, and we delighted to see Your Majesty reviewing military preparations. The palace guards stood arrayed like stars, with three thousand brave warriors ranged close by; chariots and cavalry massed like clouds, assembling a million fierce soldiers in dense ranks. Goose, crane, and fish-scale formations appeared in succession, extending lengthwise and crosswise; Fanruo bows and Pugu arrows each displayed their skill and strength. Clouds flew above the yellow imperial canopy; eagle-like ornaments [?], axes, and battle-axes gleamed. Sunlight shone upon the vermilion imperial carriage, and we delighted to behold the brilliant colors of its banners and pennants.

The troops were swift and strong, all ready to return from battle wrapped in horsehide; commanders and their aides soared like hawks, sharing the righteous resolve to volunteer for service. Their martial spirit stretched a thousand li: what need was there to brandish a sword at Yiwu? Discipline was strict throughout the Three Garrisons, surpassing even the army encamped at Xiliu. Through this [?], you displayed imperial might and struck down rebels, sweeping like lightning and racing like the wind. Thus you safeguarded the greatness of the realm and secured lasting achievement, inspiring awe abroad and maintaining order within. Truly, you fulfilled your late imperial father’s resolve to carry forward the dynastic enterprise, and extended…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
二祖創業之勳者也臣等幸邁
昌期恭逢
盛事技有慚於鳥陣何起沉砂謀寔乏乎龍
韜奚堪拔幟伏願
九德日新
五兵歲偃
握制勝之長策無怠無荒
周防患之訏謨有嚴有翼
垂裳堯殿祥光永麗于
宸樞舞羽舜階佳氣常浮于
帝座
履至尊以馭六合固千載之金甌
蒞中國而撫四夷調萬年之玉燭臣某等無
任瞻
天仰
聖欣躍屏營之至謹奉
表稱
賀以
punctuated: 二祖創業之勳者也。臣等幸邁昌期，恭逢盛事，技有慚於鳥陣，何起沉砂？謀寔乏乎龍韜，奚堪拔幟？伏願九德日新，五兵歲偃；握制勝之長策，無怠無荒；周防患之訏謨，有嚴有翼。垂裳堯殿，祥光永麗于宸樞；舞羽舜階，佳氣常浮于帝座。履至尊以馭六合，固千載之金甌；蒞中國而撫四夷，調萬年之玉燭。臣某等無任瞻天仰聖、欣躍屏營之至，謹奉表稱賀以
translation_en:
…the achievement of the two founding ancestors in establishing the dynasty. We, your servants, are fortunate to live in this flourishing age and respectfully witness this splendid event. Our skill falls short of mastery of the bird formation: how could we accomplish the stratagem of submerged sandbags? Our planning is truly deficient in the arts of the Dragon Strategies: how could we seize the enemy’s standards?

We humbly wish that your nine virtues may be renewed daily and that the five kinds of weapons may lie idle year after year. May you hold fast to the far-reaching strategy that ensures victory, without indolence or neglect; may your grand plans for preventing calamity be comprehensive, pursued with vigilance and reverence. With robes hanging loose in effortless rule in Yao’s hall, may auspicious light forever illuminate the imperial pivot; with feathered dancers performing upon Shun’s steps, may propitious vapors ever hover about the imperial throne. Occupying the most exalted position and governing all six directions, may you secure for a thousand years the golden vessel of an undivided realm. Ruling the Central Kingdom and pacifying the peoples of the four quarters, may you harmonize the seasons for ten thousand years.

We, your servants So-and-so and the others, looking up to Heaven and revering Your Sagely Majesty, cannot contain our utmost joy and reverent awe. We respectfully present this memorial of congratulation in order to…

title: 隆慶四年河南鄉試錄
text:
皇上文謨武烈敷陳切至殆服膺而有得者錄之
聖人之繼天撫世也有憲天之政以昭經
文緯武之烈必有純天之心以為揆文奮
武之原於穆不已天之神也聖人存其神
而剛柔不偏心則純乎天矣陰陽迭運天
之化也聖人達其化而德威並懋政則憲
乎天矣神以運化而鈞陶乎萬彙天所以
成大造之功心以宰政而彌綸於兩間聖
人所以弘配天之治天與聖人其致一也
===
知此可以論古帝王之治而我
祖宗之垂統貽謨
皇上之觀光揚烈其
聖文
神武與天無間者可以揄揚其盛矣粤自結繩
之政代而文運漸闢往牒所紀帝王之文
燦然矣試自明問興學者言之唐虞典樂
教胄夏商校序明倫蓋莫非崇文之化而
周之制為備焉自今觀之師氏有三德三
punctuated:
皇上文謨武烈，敷陳切至，殆服膺而有得者，錄之。

聖人之繼天撫世也，有憲天之政以昭經文緯武之烈，必有純天之心以為揆文奮武之原。於穆不已，天之神也；聖人存其神而剛柔不偏，心則純乎天矣。陰陽迭運，天之化也；聖人達其化而德威並懋，政則憲乎天矣。神以運化而鈞陶乎萬彙，天所以成大造之功；心以宰政而彌綸於兩間，聖人所以弘配天之治。天與聖人，其致一也。知此，可以論古帝王之治，而我祖宗之垂統貽謨、皇上之觀光揚烈，其聖文神武與天無間者，可以揄揚其盛矣。

粤自結繩之政代而文運漸闢，往牒所紀，帝王之文燦然矣。試自明問興學者言之：唐虞典樂教胄，夏商校序明倫，蓋莫非崇文之化，而周之制為備焉。自今觀之，師氏有三德三
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s civil plans and martial achievements are expounded with precision and earnestness. The writer has surely taken them to heart and gained an understanding of them. Include this piece.

When the sage succeeds Heaven in tending the world, he has policies modeled upon Heaven that manifest his achievements in ordering civil and military affairs. He must also possess a heart wholly attuned to Heaven as the source of his direction of civil affairs and exertion of martial power. Profound and unceasing: such is Heaven’s spiritual efficacy. When the sage preserves this efficacy, inclining neither toward firmness nor toward gentleness, his heart is wholly attuned to Heaven. Yin and yang move in alternation: such is Heaven’s transforming activity. When the sage comprehends this transformation and gives full expression to both virtue and authority, his policies are modeled upon Heaven. Through spiritual efficacy, Heaven sets transformation in motion and molds the myriad things: thus it accomplishes its great work of creation. Through his heart, the sage directs government and comprehensively orders all between Heaven and Earth: thus he extends a rule that matches Heaven. Heaven and the sage are one in their ultimate operation. Knowing this, we may discuss the government of the ancient emperors and kings. We may also extol the magnificence of our imperial ancestors’ establishment of the succession and bequest of guiding plans, and of His Majesty’s manifestation of their glory and amplification of their achievements—their sagely civil accomplishments and divine martial prowess, which accord perfectly with Heaven.

Ever since government by knotted cords was superseded and the course of civilized culture gradually opened, the civil accomplishments of emperors and kings recorded in ancient writings have shone brilliantly. Let us begin with the promotion of learning raised in your enlightened question. Under Tang and Yu, the Director of Music instructed the sons of the nobility; under Xia and Shang, the schools clarified human relationships. All of this was surely the transforming influence of honoring civil culture, but it was under Zhou that the institutions became complete.
